Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

xrdbi (development version)

Faster xr_raster()

  • xr_raster() flips rows and columns into GDAL pixel order in numpy and hands R one flat buffer, instead of converting the N-D array (which reticulate reorders to column-major) and transposing each band back in R. A 4-band 4320 x 8640 float32 stack renders in ~1.2 s, down from ~8.2 s, with identical output.

Documentation

  • Reference pages corrected in a documentation sweep: examples now use the vendored fixtures (trmm.nc, rgbsmall.tif) so they run as pasted, and no longer select an exact date that misses 12:00 times, use xvec without importing it, pass chunks = list() (a Python list) or open zarr on the dask path. Statements that compute (e.g. .mean()) are documented as running at dbSendQuery(), before the guard, which sizes only the result. ?tbl_xarray lists the supported verbs and filter forms, the guard and force, and the preview options; ?xr_raster says y and x are the last two dimensions and how srs is found; ?xr_query says character vectors are labels, not ranges.

  • ?xrdbi is now the package’s overview page: how xarray maps to DBI (tables, fields, statements, the long form), the functions by task, the guards and the four options (xrdbi.max_cells, xrdbi.max_chunks, xrdbi.print_n and xrdbi.print_preview, the last two previously undocumented), which R packages are used when installed, and the Python requirements. Every reference page links onward with a See also section, and ?dbConnect says what multidim = FALSE does for the gdalxarray engine.

  • A pkgdown site (https://mdsumner.github.io/xrdbi/), built by a GitHub Action in the ghcr.io/hypertidy/gdal-r-python image so live articles can reach GDAL and public cloud data. The reference index is grouped by task.

  • New “Get started” vignette, pre-computed: its outputs are knitted locally from vignettes/xrdbi.Rmd.orig on the bundled trmm.nc (tools/precompute.R), so it builds on CRAN without Python. New “Python environments” article: letting reticulate manage Python, your own Python, conda and pixi (and what reticulate needs there), the gdal-r-python image, and how to check what you have. The deploy step installs rsync, which the image lacks and the deploy action needs. The site’s R dependencies install with pak’s system requirements off and without upgrading the image’s packages: apt’s GDAL and GEOS beside the image’s own gave shapely the wrong libgeos_c.so.1, and a smoke step now loads sf and shapely together before the build. The build turns off dask’s array query planning, which the image turns on and under which open_mfdataset() fails; “Python environments” says how.

  • Eight more articles, built live on the site: “Querying with dplyr” (how each verb compiles and what gets read), “Parameters”, “From arrays to rows” (the shape and types of results, and when work happens), “Data sources” (a cookbook: netCDF over HTTPS, many files, zarr on Google Cloud and S3, GDAL rasters and VRTs, virtual stores), “Rasters”, “Chunk maps”, “Curvilinear grids and vector cubes”, and “Design notes”. The articles index groups them, and Get started and ?xrdbi link to them.

  • The README is now a landing page: what xrdbi is, installation, one live example on ERA5 (a value, a dplyr filter, the guard, and a global hour rendered with xr_raster()), and links to the articles. Its tutorial sections moved to the articles. tools/build-readme.sh knits it live in the gdal-r-python image. “Data sources” now opens a real icechunk repository (BRAN daily salinity on Source Cooperative, a virtual store over NCI THREDDS) in place of placeholder names, replacing the README’s icechunk example, whose repository no longer exists.

Grid tables

  • tbl() takes a grid: several data variables on one set of dimensions (tbl(con, c("sst", "ice"))), or a grid by name (tbl(con, "time,zlev,lat,lon")). A grid table has a column per member, as tidync’s hyper_tibble() does, and compiles to a Dataset statement (ds[['sst', 'ice']]). Its select() decides which members are read, plus any a filter needs; the guard counts values (cells times members); printing previews at most getOption("xrdbi.preview_members", 4) members. Variables on different grids are refused, since a statement over both would repeat values along the dimensions one lacks. A one-variable tbl() is unchanged.

  • New xr_grids() lists the grids. The "meaning" view (the default) groups data variables by their decoded dimensions as a set, with the coordinates that belong to each grid; the "storage" view groups every stored array by its stored dimensions in order, keeping the character dimension of decoded strings, and so finds the grids tidync does (16 in an Argo profile file, where the meaning view has 5).

  • xr_chunks() takes a lazy tbl() and maps what collecting it reads: for a grid table, a row per member read and chunk.

These come from a play kit tried on Argo, OISST and ERA5 before the move.

  • The README and the “Get started” vignette mention grid tables and point to the “Grid tables” section of the dplyr article.

Chunk maps

  • xr_chunks() maps start with the chunk key of a byterefs table: array, the stored variable, and, for storage chunks, dim_0 .. dim_{n-1} (integer), the chunk’s 0-based position along each stored dimension. byterefs views and zaro’s zaro_plan() use the same key, so a chunk map joins to them, one array at a time, for what they record of each chunk: presence, path and byte range (checked against zaro on zarr v2 and sharded v3 stores). Shard, dask and whole-variable maps have no dim_ keys: a first step to one plan vocabulary across array readers.

  • xr_chunks() takes a Dataset statement (ds[['sst', 'ice']].sel(...)) and maps each data variable under the one selection, a row per variable and chunk. Variables on different dimensions get missing values in the columns they lack; the guard counts every variable’s rows; chunking is one value per variable when they differ.

  • New xr_chunks() maps the storage chunks a selection touches: one row per chunk with, for each dimension, its chunk index, its 0-based start/stop index range (as in isel(slice(start, stop))) and its coordinate extent (cell edges for numeric axes), then cells and how many are selected, and a wk::rct() over the two spatial dimensions with the CRS. On a whole variable it is the chunk grid; on a selection, the chunks reading it would touch. Shapes come from encoding['preferred_chunks'], which zarr, netCDF (netCDF4, h5netcdf) and gdalxarray (classic blocks and multidimensional) all set; without it a dask grid, else one chunk. Only coordinates are read, and a max_chunks guard covers stores like ERA5 (1.3 million time chunks).

  • xr_chunks(level = "shards") maps the shards of a sharded zarr v3 array, each a stored object holding a grid of inner chunks; at the default chunk level a sharded array gets a d_shard column per dimension, the shard each chunk lives in.

  • On curvilinear grids xr_chunks() gives each chunk the envelope of its block of 2-D longitude/latitude (lon_min … lat_max, named after the coordinates, recognised by CF standard_name, units or common names), and uses it as geometry (OGC:CRS84) when the grid has no 1-D axes. Selections on index-only dimensions (isel(eta_rho=...)) are placed through the 2-D coordinates, whose value pairs are copied exactly.

Vector data cubes

  • Geometry (the geometry coordinate of an xvec vector data cube, or any column of shapely objects) arrives as wk::wkb instead of WKT text, carrying the CRS of xvec’s GeometryIndex, so it goes straight into sf (sf::st_as_sfc()). Each distinct geometry crosses once, as one byte buffer. Without the wk package it is WKT text, as before.

  • xr_raster() refuses a vector data cube with a reason (its geometry dimension has no raster rendering; use dbGetQuery()), and any non-numeric y or x axis likewise; both failed with “‘list’ object cannot be coerced to type ‘double’”.

Query parameters

  • dbSendQuery(), dbGetQuery() and xr_raster() take params, a named list whose elements become Python variables in the statement’s scope beside ds and xr: dbGetQuery(con, "ds.sst.sel(lat=lat0, method='nearest')", params = list(lat0 = -60)). Length-1 vectors become numpy scalars (I() keeps an array), longer ones numpy arrays, Date and POSIXct become datetime64 (UTC, NA as NaT), data frames pandas, and geometry (sf, sfc, wk vectors) shapely, or a geopandas GeoSeries when it has a CRS, so xvec’s extract_points() and zonal_stats() can be driven from R.

  • dbBind() evaluates a result’s statement again with new params and restarts its fetch.

  • An unbound name in a statement now says how to pass it.

CRAN preparation

  • A draft conda-forge recipe lives in tools/conda/ (not part of the R package), validated with rattler-build in a clean sandbox. Its activation script points reticulate at the environment’s Python, which reticulate otherwise ignores in favour of provisioning from PyPI (where gdalxarray cannot work); it also needs libpython, which conda-forge ships separately, and micromamba, without which reticulate cannot use a conda-layout environment where no conda binary is found (pixi, build sandboxes).

  • Loading xrdbi now declares only its core Python requirements, xarray and netCDF4 (local netCDF-3 and netCDF-4). It declared gdalxarray too, which pip can install but not make work (it needs the GDAL Python bindings), so a provisioned environment carried it, its dependencies and an xarray warning for nothing. Other engines are declared where used, e.g. reticulate::py_require(c("zarr", "gcsfs")), before or after connecting; ?xrdbi lists the common ones, and each README example declares what it needs. A new user, with no Python configured, can run the README’s OISST and ERA5 examples as written.

  • Tests that need Python skip on CRAN. Checking for the Python modules is itself what starts reticulate, which with no Python configured provisions an environment from PyPI into the user cache. The tests that need no Python (statement compilation, row windows, head blocks) still run there.

  • Every DBI method is documented: connection methods on ?XarrayConnection-class, result methods (with dbSendQuery()) on ?XarrayResult-class, driver methods on ?xarray. Every exported function documents its return value and has examples; those needing Python are in \dontrun{}.

  • DESCRIPTION declares the Python requirement in SystemRequirements, links xarray, credits the GDAL/OGR contributors for the vendored test fixtures (see inst/COPYRIGHTS), and requires reticulate >= 1.41.0, the first release with py_require() (which .onLoad() calls).

README

  • The README’s “Verbs and semantics” section showed only errors (the chunk-map section had reused and closed its connection, and a chunk-wide error = TRUE let the build pass). Each example now has its own connection and only the intended guard error is allowed. Also corrected: a filter example used the R object’s name for the variable, NA vs NaN, 0-d results, the laziness claims, and the chunks note now follows the ERA5 example it is about.

  • The README gains a live chunk-map section: the 1024 x 1024 block grid of a Sentinel-2 Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF, and a window’s touched blocks shaded by how much of each it reads (figure in man/figures/).

  • The README is now README.Rmd, built live with devtools::build_readme() against the remote examples (OISST over HTTPS, ARCO ERA5 on GCS, the OISST multidim VRT via gdalxarray), and it gains a dplyr section.

Fixes

  • Rows render from GDAL rasters opened with gdalxarray’s classic mode (multidim = FALSE). Their x and y carry rasterix’s RasterIndex, which to_dataframe() cannot cast to pandas, so every row query failed; a scalar y selection, which leaves x with no index at all, failed differently. Rendering now gives such coordinates plain pandas indexes first. xr_raster() and xr_chunks() still read the original indexes.

  • tbl() filters on a GDAL raster’s y, which runs north to south, select the right side. The direction check read ds.indexes, failed on the RasterIndex and assumed ascending, so filter(y > ...) returned nothing. The direction check, the strict-bound trim and the empty-result hint now use the coordinate’s to_index(), which works for any index.

  • Numbers in compiled statements are written to round-trip exactly. At 15 significant digits a value fetched from the data, such as a coordinate (-22.941163999999997), became -22.941164, and a strict bound at it kept its own cell. Values as typed (18, -44.83) are written as before.

  • A vector cube’s geometry keeps its CRS when the geometry coordinate has geopandas’ geometry extension dtype, as the result of xvec’s zonal_stats() does. Only object-dtype coordinates were looked at, so the values arrived as wk::wkb() but without the CRS.

  • collect() on a tbl() takes max_cells, like the other guarded functions. It went into ... and was ignored, so collect(x, max_cells = 10) read everything. as.data.frame() takes the same arguments and now gives a plain data frame (it was defined twice, the second definition returning a tibble).

  • A POSIXct in a tbl() filter or xr_query() is compiled as its instant in UTC, as xarray stores times. It was written as wall-clock time in the object’s own zone, so a bound in e.g. Australia/Hobart selected 11 hours off. (params already converted to UTC.)

  • xr_raster() and xr_chunks() find a CRS from a CF grid_mapping variable’s parameters (grid_mapping_name and the rest), through pyproj when installed, as a last resort: authored WKT (crs_wkt, spatial_ref) anywhere still comes first.

  • xr_raster() finds the CRS that gdalxarray records in an xproj CRSIndex (its crs coordinate has no attributes), or that a rasterix RasterIndex carries; srs was empty for gdalxarray rasters.

  • A 0-d data variable renders with its scalar coordinates ahead of its value, as to_dataframe() would: a single cell, or a nearest-point lookup, keeps where it is (time, lat, lon, …) instead of only the value. A 0-d coordinate still renders just itself.

  • xr_raster() accepts regular grids stored as float32. Their rounding (about 1.2e-7 of each value) made the steps of e.g. a 0.44 degree rotated-pole grid vary by 1e-5 of the step, failing a fixed 1e-6 tolerance; the tolerance now scales with the coordinate’s precision, and the step is the mean over the axis.

  • The cell guard never fired above 2^31 cells, so it missed exactly the reads it exists to stop. reticulate converts a Python int that large into a wrapped R integer (2^31 became NA, 17 billion became -179,869,184), so dbReadTable(con, "sst") on the full OISST record started rendering 17 billion cells instead of erroring. Sizes now cross as doubles, in dbFetch(), dbReadTable() and collect(), and guard messages print counts in full.

  • Printing a connection cuts the variable list to the console width, with a total (ERA5 has 273 data variables).

  • show_query() backticks non-syntactic names in the R steps line, so it is valid R.

Faster, type-faithful conversion to R

  • dbFetch(), dbGetQuery(), dbReadTable() and collect() now convert the rendered pandas frame column by column from numpy buffers instead of with reticulate’s whole-DataFrame conversion. A 10M-row fetch with a time dimension drops from ~22 s to ~1.2 s; nearly all the old cost was reticulate’s handling of a datetime column.

  • Types that were wrong before now convert properly: NaT is NA (it was 1677-09-21 in a numpy route), timedeltas are difftime seconds (they were NA dates), pandas string columns such as string coordinates are character (they were left as Python objects), categoricals are factors (they made the fetch error), cftime values from non-standard calendars are ISO strings (they were a list of Python objects), bytes are decoded, and nullable integers and booleans keep NA.

  • For a plain DataArray (the usual ds.var.sel(...) statement, and tbl() pipelines whose filters all push down to .sel()), the long form is now built in R: only the values, flattened in C order, cross from Python, and the coordinate columns are repeated with rep(). The 10M-row fetch drops again to ~0.55 s, and dbFetch(n = ) builds only the rows asked for (10 chunks of 1M rows: ~0.4 s in total). The output is identical to the pandas render. Datasets, 0-d and empty results, MultiIndex coordinates and pandas-stage statements still go through the pandas render.

  • head() and select() in tbl() pipelines no longer force a pandas stage unless a filter on data values needs one. They apply in R to the fetched rows, and head(n) first narrows the selection to the leading block holding its first n rows. head(10) on a lazy 207M-cell variable collects in 0.07 s and reads one chunk; before, it tripped the cell guard, and with force it rendered the whole selection in pandas. show_query() and the printed tbl list the R steps.

  • collect(force = TRUE) works again for pipelines that compile to a plain xarray selection. collect() honoured force, but dbFetch() checked the guard again without it. The collect guard now counts the cells actually read (strict trims and the head() block included).

  • Datasets now take the R-built path too, mirroring xarray’s to_dataframe(): rows are every combination of the Dataset’s dims, and each non-index variable is broadcast across them, whether or not the variables share dims. 10M rows x 2 variables: 0.78 s instead of 1.71 s, identical output. Stacked (MultiIndex) dims, other non-dim indexes and pandas extension arrays still use the pandas render.

  • The cell guard now applies to Datasets. A Dataset has no .size, so the guard silently never fired: dbGetQuery(con, "ds") on a large store would try to load all of it. It now counts rows x data variables.

  • A 0-d Dataset (every dim selected to one value) renders as one row; it errored in to_dataframe().

  • tbl() filters on non-dimension coordinates (2-D lat/lon of a curvilinear grid, a 1-D coordinate along time) narrow the read to the index block holding every cell that passes, computed from the coordinates at collect time; the pandas query still applies them exactly inside the block. On a 40 x 60 grid a lat/lon box reads 507 of 7,200 cells. The collect guard counts the narrowed read, and the preview’s note no longer blames value filters for coordinate filters.

  • Strict bounds on a dimension in tbl() filters (lat > 18, time < as.Date(...)) no longer drop to a pandas .query(). The inclusive .sel() hull is trimmed with a boolean .isel() on the dimension’s index, which uses the same pandas comparison as the query, so date strings keep their meaning. The statement stays a DataArray and takes the R-built path: 4.8M rows collect in 0.43 s instead of 1.16 s, with identical output. Filters on data variables, select() and head() still use the pandas stage.

  • Datetimes without a zone now carry tzone = "UTC", so they display as the instant the source means regardless of the session zone. Timezone-aware datetimes keep their zone.

  • The GDAL autotest fixture tests had been skipping because of a stale helper call; they run again.

xr_raster(): raster rendering of a result

  • Printing a tbl now renders a lazy preview - sizes from metadata, the first cells clamped to at most one chunk read, tibble-formatted, with options(xrdbi.print_preview = FALSE) to opt out; and the compiled pandas stage routes through the connection’s renderer (.pipe(_xrdbi_render), visible in show_query()), so coordinate tables, 0-d results, and empty selections behave identically in tbl pipelines and raw statements.

  • New xr_raster() renders a slab in gdalraster’s in-memory raster format: a plain vector of pixel values (left-to-right, top-to-bottom, band-sequential; as_list = TRUE for a list of band vectors) with a gis attribute carrying type, bbox, dim, srs, and datatype – interchangeable with the output of gdalraster::read_ds(), and compatible with ximage::ximage().

  • Where dbFetch() renders the tidy long-form data frame, this is a sibling rendering on the same lazy result: xr_raster(res) on an XarrayResult, or xr_raster(con, statement). The DBI contract is untouched. The array is a rendering format; so is the data frame; so is this.

  • Shapes: 2-D (y, x) single band, or 3-D (band, y, x) band-sequential stack (a time series of slabs; dim order preserved, so band b is unambiguously e.g. time[b]). 4-D and higher refuse with an error carrying the explicit flatten recipe (e.g. .stack(band=('zlev','time')).transpose('band','lat','lon')), because the gis format has no band-names field and silent flattening would invent an ordering the object cannot record. y and x are positionally the last two dims (CF/xarray convention). Dimension coordinates must be regular (“warp first” otherwise); the half-cell bbox expansion assumes cell centres; ascending or descending order on either axis is handled. The xrdbi.max_cells guard applies.

CRS: lifted

  • gis$srs is populated by a verbatim lift, in order of specificity: a spatial_ref/crs coordinate on the object ; the variable’s CF grid_mapping pointer followed into the parent dataset (grid-mapping variables are 0-d data variables and do not propagate through selection); or conventional names at the dataset level (catching statements that strip attrs, e.g. arithmetic). Only an authored crs_wkt/spatial_ref WKT string is ever read; CF projection-parameter interpretation is deliberately out of scope.

Self-contained test fixtures

  • A curated set of GDAL autotest files (four netCDFs exercising CF packing, descending latitude, and grid mappings, plus the canonical byte.tif and 3-band rgbsmall.tif) is vendored flat into inst/extdata/autotest/ (~100 KB) with a PROVENANCE file recording source paths, commit, and the MIT/X license. tools/update-fixtures.R re-vendors from a checkout; the GDAL_AUTOTEST environment variable is now only needed when updating fixtures, never for testing.

  • The rotated_pole.nc tests name their engine. Without one, a Python missing netCDF4 opened the file with gdalxarray, and the grid-mapping test skipped as an engine difference instead of saying netCDF4 was missing. netcdf4 keeps projection as a 0-d variable; a new test checks that gdalxarray’s classic mode puts the rotated-pole CRS in xr_raster()’s srs.

xrdbi 0.0.1.9000 (development)

Initial DBI backend for xarray: the “database” is a live Python session (reticulate) holding an xarray object.

Features

  • dplyr verbs over any xarray-openable source; dimension filters push down to oriented label slices, value filters apply before conversion; one inspectable python statement. tbl(con, var) returns a lazy spec; filter/select/head accumulate; collect() compiles ONE python statement and runs it through dbGetQuery. Dimension predicates push down to an inclusive .sel hull (fewer chunks touched); strict bounds and data-variable predicates remain as a pandas .query applied before conversion to R (pushdown with residuals). At collect, each hull dimension is probed for direction and the slice oriented to match, so range filters work identically on ascending and descending coordinates. show_query() prints the compiled python.

  • Three connect forms via dbConnect(xarray(), ...): a dsn string that xarray can open (open function selectable via open =, keyword arguments passed through), a builder function receiving the xarray module (for icechunk sessions, virtualizarr, multi-step opens), or an existing Python object adopted from the session.

  • Statements are Python expressions evaluated with ds and xr in scope. dbSendQuery() is lazy (builds the selection graph, moves no bytes); rendering to the tidy long-form data frame happens at dbFetch(), paginated Python-side.

  • xr_query() compiles a structured spec (vars, sel, isel, method, tail) to an inspectable Python expression string. isel is zero-based, faithfully: values are interpolated, not translated.

  • Coordinates are tables too: dbListTables() lists ds.variables (data variables and coordinates); the data/coords split remains available via dbGetInfo(). Dimension coordinates render as a single column of their values; scalar coordinates and scalar results as a one-row frame; a non-dimension coordinate’s self-reference is deduplicated.

  • All results funnel through a single Python-side renderer installed at connect, covering Dataset, DataArray (including 0-d), and plain Python values.

  • Kind messages on empty results: when a selection collapses a dimension to zero, the parent coordinate is inspected and the message reports a DESCENDING coordinate (label slices follow coordinate order; try slice(hi, lo)) or the coordinate span (catches out-of-range values and -180..180 vs 0..360 longitude conventions).

  • Whole-variable reads are guarded against accidental terabyte renderings (options(xrdbi.max_cells = ), or force = TRUE).

  • Escape hatches: xr_dataset(con) and xr_module(con) return the live Python handles.

  • Transactions (dbBegin/dbCommit/dbRollback) error with a pointer to the intended mapping onto icechunk sessions and commits.

Fixes

  • Statement scope is built with py_dict() and explicit character keys; reticulate::dict() resolves argument names against calling frame variables, which made the local ds Dataset a dict key (unhashable) (#nn).

  • Removed use of a nonexistent reticulate::py_slice(); pagination uses builtins slice.

  • 0-d renderings use values[()] rather than .item(), which returns raw integer nanoseconds for ns-precision datetimes.

Documentation

  • Worked examples against real sources: OISST NetCDF over HTTPS (h5netcdf), ARCO ERA5 zarr v3 on anonymous GCS (including the descending-latitude gotcha, kept in as a lesson), and an OISST daily multidim VRT mosaic via the gdalxarray engine (deferred credential errors, connection-as-snapshot semantics).

  • Guidance on chunks: omit for lazy zarr-backed arrays and fast connects; chunks = dict() wraps variables in dask at native storage chunking, which for finely-chunked stores can cost minutes of task graph construction (observed: 96s vs 7s on a 1-timestep-per-chunk store). Note the differing defaults of open_dataset (None) and open_zarr (“auto”).

Planned

  • dbplyr-style laziness via tbl() in the dtplyr/duckplyr mould: capture dplyr verbs, compile to xr_query() specs (filter on dim coords to sel/isel, value predicates to where, summarise to reductions).

  • Alternate renderings as sibling verbs on a result, leaving the dbFetch() data frame contract intact: xr_array() (values plus dims and coords, skipping the pandas hop) and xr_raster() (SpatRaster from a regular-grid slab).

  • DataTree groups as schemas, write support (to_zarr / icechunk commit), registry integration (dbConnect(xarray(), dsn(...))).
